newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine Congress tax changes may cost $400 mln.
newsitem.headline: Argentine Congress tax changes may cost $400 mln.

text.p: Economy Minister Roque Fernandez told Argentine economists Wednesday that Congress' changes to his tax package to be voted by deputies will reduce its impact on the 1996 budget by $400 million at most.

"The minister is absolutely convinced that the fiscal cost of the changes introduced to his package by parliament will be very low; he quantified the difference from the original at $350-400 million," said Miguel Angel Broda, one of the 30 top Argentine economists summoned for talks with Fernandez.

The Chamber of Deputies was due to debate later Wednesday the much-altered fiscal package that Fernandez first announced on August 21 when he estimated it would reduce the 1996 budget deficit by $1.6 billion.

Since then, however, the package has been watered down and delayed at the committee stage by lower house congressmen, who removed extensions to value added tax and a rise in women's retirement age, and are undecided on exporters' refunds cuts.

The Deputies' Budget Committee also removed an article giving the central government exclusive access to revenue from new taxes on diesel, gasoline and natural gas, rather than sharing it with the provinces. But Peronist deputies say they depend on the Senate to decide on tax sharing.

Nora Balzarotti, an economist from the private analysts' group Proeco, told reporters the meeting concentrated on the so-called Second Reform of State, designed to streamline the administration. Fernandez told economists he hopes to save $1.3 billion on the 1997 budget through the reform.

She described that as welcome news, but added: "The bad thing was it confirmed the changes to the tax package and that the abolition of VAT exemptions was scrapped. One of the basic requirements for making the system more efficient is for no sector to remain without VAT."

Interior Minister Carlos Corach, speaking in New York, tried to play down the alterations to the fiscal program, calling them "changes in secondary aspects." He forecast that both houses of Congress would approve the bill by October.
"I am sure that all the Peronist Party -- 99 percent of the Peronist Party -- is behind the President's austerity program," Corach said.
